summary:
Borno State stands under Nigeria's national framework, and its criminalisation of same-sex conduct rests independently on Borno's own legislation. The state's statute on prostitution, homosexuality, brothels and other sexual immoralities was signed by Governor Kachalla on 10 December 2000 and gazetted in Borno State Gazette No. 42 Vol. 26 on 18 October 2001. Section 3 makes engaging in prostitution, lesbianism, a homosexual act or pimping an offence in the state. Section 7 provides that any person who 'engages in sexual intercourse with another person of the same gender shall upon conviction be punished with death'. Section 4 deems all brothels closed on commencement, and section 9 assigns jurisdiction over these offences to the Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts.

The death penalty in section 7 is stated in the statute's own text without any religious qualification, so the maximum penalty in Borno does not depend on the applicant's faith, unlike the Sharia layer, which Human Rights Watch records as extending to Muslims.

Borno enacted a second, parallel layer of its own. The state's Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 was signed into law on 3 March 2003, with no operation date or gazette identified in the sourcebook that lists it. The Borno text was obtained only in May 2006, after that volume's annotation had been completed, which is why Borno does not appear among the individually annotated codes; the parallel Sharia layer for Borno rests on a Borno-specific enactment rather than on federal or umbrella coverage.

Human Rights Watch's 2004 report lists Borno among the twelve northern states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law.

The UK Home Office country-of-origin information note of June 2025 states that Islamic law applies to Muslims in the twelve northern states, including Borno, and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women. The maximum penalty for 'sodomy' for men is death in all twelve states, and penalties for 'lesbianism' range from death to flogging and imprisonment. The note carries a dedicated section on the enforcement of Sharia provisions and on the attitude of the hisbah, the morality police operating in these states.
tangentialFactors:
Borno is one of twelve northern states carrying the same Sharia criminal layer, so the death-penalty exposure recorded for the northern states as a group by the UK Home Office in June 2025 is not an outlier feature of Borno alone. Borno is distinguished by having enacted that maximum in its own secular morality statute as well, through section 7 of the 2000 act.

The comparative sourcebook that catalogues enacted Sharia Penal Codes across northern Nigeria does not individually annotate Borno, because the state's text reached the compilers in May 2006 after the volume had been finalised. That is a documentation gap in the comparative literature, not an absence of enacted law: the code is listed, dated to its signature on 3 March 2003, and separately reproduced for the 2000 morality statute.
localsOnly:
For residents of Borno, the jurisdictional arrangement in section 9 of the 2000 statute places these offences before the Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts, so prosecution runs through the state's ordinary and Sharia court structure rather than through any single tribunal.

Human Rights Watch records that Shari'a courts in Borno hold criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law, and the UK Home Office note of June 2025 documents the hisbah, the morality police, as an enforcement actor under the Sharia provisions in the northern states. Both layers apply within Borno's own territory to Muslim residents.

Section 4 of the 2000 statute deemed all brothels in the state closed on commencement of the act, a standing closure provision rather than an offence requiring a complaint.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Borno-specific enforcement incident, arrest, prosecution, custody placement or act of violence against a trans or gender-nonconforming person is documented in this inventory, and no date can be given for any such event in Borno. The most recent Borno-specific legal instrument sourced here is the Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, signed 3 March 2003.

Whether the death penalty enacted in section 7 of Borno's 2000 statute, or the death penalty available under the Sharia layer, has been imposed or carried out in Borno is not sourced here. Unresolved as well: the operation date and gazette reference for the Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, and the full text of that code, which the sourcebook records as obtained only in May 2006.

The specific content of the UK Home Office note's section on hisbah attitudes, and any documented hisbah conduct toward trans or gender-nonconforming people in Borno, is not reproduced in this inventory and remains unverified here.
